title: Wire-format serialization overhead probe — ingress/egress lab notes (Jan 2027)
body:
Goal:
Run tightly controlled microbenchmarks to quantify per-chunk serialization and wire-format costs across three common paths: (A) direct gRPC (h2) to backend, (B) gRPC-Web (JSON-wrapped frames) through Envoy HTTP/1.1 proxy, (C) gRPC h2 through an edge proxy that does TLS termination + buffering. We want concrete numbers (median, p95, p99) for small vs large chunk sizes and to capture syscall/flush behavior that affects tail latency.

Motivation / why this matters:
- Many client SDKs default to small streaming frames when sending prompts and tokens are emitted in tiny increments; these tiny writes interact badly with proxies and OS TCP coalescing.
- We suspect that wire-format wrapping (JSON envelope used by some frontends / gRPC-web) adds both CPU serialization cost and extra bytes on the wire which amplifies proxy buffering and backpressure.
- Micro-tail latency (~p99) has outsized product impact; we need prioritized mitigations.

Testbed summary:
- Backend: inference runtime on g4dn.12xlarge-equivalent (8xA10G) in same AZ. Server binary built with -O2; pprof enabled.
- Proxy: Envoy stable build (v1.28) configured in two roles: HTTP/1.1 gRPC-web translation path and TLS-terminating edge proxy (http2 upstream).
- Clients: synthetic Go harness (net/http2 and grpc-go), and a JS gRPC-web shim (node). Harness instrumented to emit span ids and measure client-side enqueue->first-byte->last-byte.
- Wire captures: tcpdump + tshark for representative traces; strace on client and server to capture syscalls; heap/CPU pprof on server.
- Workloads: 1) small-chunk stream (mean chunk 512B, 80% chunks <1KB), 2) medium (4KB), 3) large (16KB). Each run: 30k requests at steady concurrency 50, ramped to 200 for stress runs.

Key commands used (notes to self):
- client run: go run ./bench --mode=grpc --chunksize=512 --concurrency=50 --rate=unlimited
- grpc-web: node bench-web.js --endpoint https://edge-proxy:8443 --chunksize=512
- capture: sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w /tmp/ws.pcap 'tcp port 443 or tcp port 80' &
- strace sampling: sudo strace -f -p <pid> -tt -e write,sendto,sendmsg -o /tmp/strace-client.log -c  

Observations (raw):
- Direct gRPC (A) median RTT per-chunk: ~0.45ms (512B), p95: 1.1ms, p99: 5.2ms.
- gRPC-Web via Envoy translating to JSON frames (B) median: ~0.95ms (512B), p95: 3.6ms, p99: 18.6ms.
- Edge TLS+buffering proxy (C) median: ~0.78ms (512B), p95: 2.8ms, p99: 12.3ms.
- For 4KB chunks differences narrow: A median 0.6ms, B median 0.8ms, C median 0.75ms. p99s also closer for larger chunks.
- Strace shows many small write syscalls from client when chunk size is small; when client coalesced writes (local buffer to 4KB) syscall count dropped ~70% and p99 improved by ~35% for path C.

Interpretation / hypotheses:
1) Serialization CPU cost: JSON envelope + base64 framing in gRPC-Web path adds ~40–70us per chunk for the server side (observed in pprof CPU samples), which matches the extra median we see for path B.
2) Proxy buffering and head-of-line: small frames hit Envoy’s downstream buffering heuristics, which introduce variable delay before translation and flush to upstream; this explains the large p99 amplification for path B.
3) Syscall and Nagle interactions: many small writes lead to kernel-level coalescing (TCP small-packet amplification) and interactions with TCP_CORK/TCP_NODELAY. Explicit coalescing at the SDK yielded big wins.
4) TLS termination cost: reassembling many small TLS records at proxy is CPU-expensive and reduces batching; combined with Envoy filters it increases tail.

Concrete numbers to cite (best-effort averages across 3 runs):
- Extra median overhead introduced by JSON-wrapping (B vs A) at 512B: +0.5ms median, +13.4ms p99.
- Syscall reduction (coalesce->4KB) improved p99 by 35% on path C and ~45% on path B.
- CPU samples show ~4–8% of server CPU taken by JSON encode/decode for small-chunk-heavy workload.

Short experiment notes (gotchas):
- Envoy config matters: enabling http1/1 keepalive window and stream idle timeouts changed p99 substantially. Our baseline used default timeouts which penalized tiny idle streams.
- gRPC-go and grpc-web shims behave differently under backpressure: grpc-go tends to block the sender on full write buffer; the js shim buffered and produced many small writes.
- TLS session resumption was disabled in some earlier runs by mistake — invalidated first pass, discarded those numbers.

Actionable mitigations to try (ranked):
1) SDK default change: coalesce small frames in client to a 2–4KB write buffer before sending. Low risk, large win.
2) On Envoy: tune downstream buffer and set early-flush for gRPC-web translation path to avoid artificial batching windows. Medium risk (requires QA).
3) Use binary framing for edge->backend where possible (avoid JSON envelope) — bigger engineering lift but reduces both CPU and bytes-on-wire.
4) Add guidance to docs: avoid <1KB default chunking for production; provide code snippets to coalesce.
5) Investigate enabling TCP_CORK/TCP_QUICKACK on servers where applicable to reduce small-packet amplification.

Next steps / experiments planned:
- Repeat the 512B profile with a production-like mix of KV-cache warmup (cold/hot) to measure interplay with backend latency.
- Run same test with quantized model CPU paths (smaller token compute) to ensure serialization overhead remains meaningful when compute time drops.
- Test an Envoy build with the json-translation filter removed to measure pure overhead of translation code path (isolated CPU cost).
- Prototype an SDK change that batches outgoing user frames; run A/B in staging for 1 week.

Unresolved questions / discussion points:
- Are there cases where small-frame semantics are necessary (e.g., real-time typing UX) such that we cannot coalesce without harming UX? We need product input.
- How does HTTP/2 flow-control window tuning interact with our streaming patterns at scale across multiple proxies?
- Is there an opportunity to get better telemetry (per-chunk tracing) without imposing measurement overhead?

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally a working lab notebook. Numbers are from controlled runs but not a final benchmarking report. Please call out any blind spots (other proxy types, cloud LB configs) and if you can reproduce on GCP LB (we tested AWS infra only here).
- If we proceed with SDK default changes, we should add a feature flag and dashboards to track regressions (tokens/sec, p99).

References / links (in-body):
- Bench PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/benchmarks/pull/432 (run scripts + harness)
- Related ticket: jira:ENG-1245 (investigate streaming tail latency)
- Slack convo: #serving-runtime thread 2027-01-13

Author notes: felt like a combination of kernel/syscall noise + Envoy buffering when looking at the traces. Biggest low-hanging fruit is client-side coalescing — low risk and measurable.

End of lab note.
